messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Polar coordinates
parts: When using polar coordinates, it is possible to turn a unimodal posterior into a bimodal posterior -- for example, if you have theta going from -pi to +pi, and the posterior distribution for theta overlaps the cutpoint at +/- pi. Is there any good way of dealing with this problem in Stan, other than "don't use polar coordinates"?

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Polar coordinates
parts:
Don’t use polar coordinates.

The problem is actually worse because the Jacobian
is an infinite sum that can’t be calculated exactly.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Polar coordinates
parts:
Polar coordinates are not isomorphic to R^{2} —
you’re missing the origin.  Topologically polar
coordinates describe an annulus and not a plane.
The difference is small and doesn’t really affect
expectations or probabilities, but it does prevent
one from mapping a distribution back and forth
exactly.

The way to see that is to compute the Jacobian
and remember that you have to sum over _all_
possible zeros of the transformation.  Because
sin and cos are multivalued this leads to an
infinite number of terms, one for each possible
choice of phase.  To collapse all of those terms
into a single term you have to ignore the hole
at zero which, as I note above, doesn’t make
a practical difference but it does affect things
theoretically.

In any case, there are well-behaved transformations 
from R^{2} -> R^{2} that do map a unimodal
density to a multimodal density so you do have
to be careful with nonlinear transformations, even
ignoring the topological issues with polar coordinates.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Polar coordinates
parts:
There's a chapter in the manual on circular statistics
that answers some of Ben B's and Kevin's questions.

The unit_vector[N] type puts you on the unit hypersphere in
N dimensions. It uses N parameters despite there only
being (N - 1) degrees of freedom (there is no isomorphism from
R^(N-1) to the hypersphere as Michael points out). Rather
than this being improper, it controls the extra parameter with
a latent normal distribution to make sure the result is uniform
over the unit vectors. So you get the continuity bit of the
morphism, but not monotonicity in the metric (a point can be
more distant in R^N from another point and still be closer
in the transform to S^(N-1) [the hypersphere].

- Bob
